newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: INTERVIEW-Union sees strife if Lisbon tough on pay.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Union sees strife if Lisbon tough on pay.

text.p: Portugal's top public sector trade union official on Thursday said the 1997 wages round starting next week could end in conflict if the government offered less than the 4.25 percent agreed for 1996.

Asked how unions would respond if the government stuck to its position of offering a lower wages increase than set for 1996, Carlos Mamede, head of the 300,000-strong Frente Comum, said in an interview: "There will certainly be conflict."
He declined to elaborate but said the Socialist government did not have to prune civil servants' salaries in order to meet economic targets to join a single European currency in 1999.
Frente Comum represents about half of Portugal's estimated 500,000 to 800,000 civil servants.
"The government does not have to cut public sector salaries to meet convergence targets for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU)," Mamede told Reuters.
"It should boost revenues instead by raising the efficiency of tax collection and cracking down on widespread tax evasion."

Arnaldo Silva, the government's number two public sector wage negotiator, told Reuters last week that public sector wage increases next year must be below the 4.25 percent agreed for 1996 as tight control of state spending was essential for Portugal's hopes of joining the single currency.

Frente Comum, linked to the Communist-dominated General Confederation of Portuguese Workers (CGTP), is demanding a seven percent increase in the 1997 public sector wages round starting on October 9, Mamede said.
The two other union groups taking part in the talks are demanding a 4.5 percent increase.
The unions' demands are above the government's target to bring inflation down to 2.25 to 2.50 percent by December 1997 from a forecast 3.0 percent at the end of 1996.
Mamede said the demand was justified by a 4.6 percent fall in civil servant purchasing power over the past five years and lags in public sector wage raises over the private sector.
"The average civil servant's salary in Portugal is about a third of the European average," he said.

Mamede, who expected the 1997 public sector wage talks to be concluded by the end of November, said his group would press to erase the differential between the national and public sector minimum wage in Portugal.
The public sector minimum wage was 4.5 percent below the national level of 54,600 escudos ($353) per month, he said.

Mamede welcomed remarks this week by Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco who rejected recommendations by the International Monetary Fund to cut civil service jobs in order to meet EMU convergence targets.
But he said the distribution of workers across the ministries was inefficient and called for a restructuring.
